title: Recurrent Neural Networks
oneLiner: A recurrent network reads a sequence one step at a time and carries a memory (the hidden state) from each step to the next.

what.html:
A recurrent neural network (RNN) is a network with a loop. It reads a sequence (words, sensor readings, audio frames) one element at a time. At every step it combines the new input with a hidden state, a fixed-size summary of everything it has seen so far, and passes the updated state on to the next step.

Everyday versionReading a novel, you don't re-read every earlier page before each new sentence. You carry a running mental summary ("who's who, what just happened") and update it as you go. The hidden state is that running summary, and the RNN uses the same reading habits on every page.

GRUs and LSTMs are RNNs with gates: small learned switches that decide what to keep, what to overwrite and what to output, so the memory lasts much longer.

why.html:
• Order matters. "Dog bites man" and "man bites dog" use the same words.
  • Inputs have different lengths. A feed-forward network expects a fixed-size input.
  • The clue may be far back. In "I grew up in France … I speak fluent ___", the word that decides "French" came many words earlier.
  • The same pattern can appear anywhere. Sharing one set of weights across all positions lets what is learnt at one position help at every other.

how.title: Sequences everywhere
how.html: Text, speech, video, stock prices, temperatures, DNA: in all of them the order carries meaning. Some dependencies are short ("the clouds are in the sky"), some long ("I grew up in France … I speak fluent French"). A good model remembers what matters and forgets what doesn't.

how.title: Predicting the next item from the past
how.html: Any sequence's probability can be written as a chain: P(first word) × P(second | first) × P(third | first two) × … This is exact, but the history keeps growing. The Markov shortcut only looks at the last one or two items (bigram/trigram): cheap, but it forgets "cat" by the time it predicts "mat".

how.title: Summarise the past in a hidden state
how.html: Instead of a fixed window, keep a running summary ht that is updated from the old summary and the new input: ht = f(xt, ht−1). Its size never grows, however long the sequence. In the weather example, a model that only sees today's 21 °C predicts 20.8 °C; a state that remembers "it has been cooling for two days" predicts lower.

how.title: The RNN: one cell, reused at every step
how.html: At each step: mix the previous state and the new input with weights, squash with tanh to get the new state; turn the state into scores for the next word with another weight matrix and a softmax. Unrolled over time it looks like a very deep network, but every copy uses the same three weight matrices, so the parameter count doesn't depend on the sequence length.

how.title: Counting parameters
how.html: For 100-dimensional inputs, 256 hidden units and a 10,000-word vocabulary, a vanilla RNN has 2,661,392 parameters, and 96% of them sit in the output layer that scores the 10,000 words.

how.title: A forward pass by hand
how.html: With the slide's small weights and h₀ = 0, the first input (1.0, 0.5) gives h₁ ≈ (0.635, 0.462, 0.291); the second input (0.8, 1.2) together with h₁ gives h₂ ≈ (0.825, 0.780, 0.592). The second state depends on the first input through h₁: that's memory. tanh keeps states between −1 and 1; ReLU can make them blow up.

how.title: Training: score every prediction
how.html: At each step the model predicts the next item; the loss is how surprised it was by the right answer (cross-entropy), added up over the sequence. Minimising it is the same as maximising the probability the model gives to the training sequences. eaverage loss is the perplexity: roughly how many words the model is choosing between.

how.title: Backpropagation through time
how.html: Unroll the network, run ordinary backprop from the last step back to the first, and add up the gradient for each shared weight from every step. A state's gradient gets two contributions: from its own output, and from everything it influenced later.

how.title: Why plain RNNs forget: vanishing gradients
how.html: Going one step back multiplies the gradient by roughly (activation slope) × (size of Whh). If that is 0.4, after 20 steps the signal is 0.4²⁰ ≈ 10⁻⁸: the early words get no learning signal. If it's above 1 the gradient explodes instead (fix: gradient clipping).

how.title: Reading both ways: bidirectional RNNs
how.html: "I met Paris in Paris": you need the words after each "Paris" to tell the person from the city. A bidirectional RNN runs one RNN left-to-right and another right-to-left and joins their states. Great when the whole sentence is available (tagging, classification); useless for live prediction, where the future hasn't happened yet.

how.title: Stacking layers: deep RNNs
how.html: Feed one RNN's states into another RNN. Lower layers pick up simple patterns (characters, short trends), higher layers more abstract ones (words, phrases, seasons). Gradients now have to travel back through time and through depth, so 2–4 layers is the practical range.

how.title: The GRU: two gates
how.html: The reset gate decides how much of the old state to use when proposing new content; the update gate decides how much of the old state to keep versus replace with that proposal. With the update gate near 1 the GRU simply copies its memory forward, which also gives gradients a clean path back.

how.title: The LSTM: a separate memory lane
how.html: The LSTM keeps a cell state (long-term memory) next to the hidden state (what it shows). Three gates: forget (erase parts of memory), input (write new information), output (what to reveal). Memory is updated by adding, not by multiplying through a weight matrix, so with the forget gate open, information and gradients can travel across hundreds of steps.

how.title: GRU or LSTM?
how.html: GRU: 2 gates, ~25% fewer parameters, faster, good up to ~100 steps. LSTM: 3 gates and a separate cell, more parameters, the safest choice for very long sequences. In practice they often perform similarly, so try both.

how.title: Forecasting time series
how.html: Feed the last 7 days of temperature, humidity and pressure into an LSTM and predict tomorrow's temperature (many-to-one). Train with mean squared error and report RMSE or MAE in degrees. Always compare with "tomorrow = today": a model that can't beat that isn't useful.

demo.html: Step through the slide's forward pass: press Step for t = 1, then again for t = 2 and the numbers match the slides. Then change the inputs and keep stepping. Notice that every box uses the same weights, and each new state depends on all the earlier inputs.

example.html:
Next-word prediction: "The cat sat on the ___": the hidden state after "the" summarises the whole sentence and the softmax puts high probability on "mat".

Weather: from 20, 22, 25, 24, 21 °C, a one-step model says 20.8 °C; a trend-aware state says it's still cooling. The slides' LSTM forecaster reads 7 days of (temperature, humidity, pressure) with 64 hidden units.

Supplementary In telecom networks, GRU/LSTM models forecast hourly cell load and flag KPI anomalies when the observed value falls far outside the forecast band; bidirectional models label each alarm in a recorded sequence.

misunderstandings: An RNN has a different set of weights for each time step.
The same weights are reused at every step; unrolling just draws copies of one cell.
They greatly reduce it via the additive cell path, but very long dependencies remain hard; attention (next module) addresses this.
They need the whole sequence first, so they can't be used for live prediction or language generation.
The hidden state stores the whole history exactly.
It is a fixed-size, lossy summary; what it keeps depends on training.
Gradients must flow through time and depth; beyond 2–4 layers gains usually vanish.
takeaways: An RNN reads sequences step by step, carrying a fixed-size hidden state h_t = tanh(W_hh h_{t−1} + W_hx x_t + b).
The same weights are shared across all time steps, so any sequence length works with a fixed number of parameters.
Training is backpropagation through time: unroll, backprop, sum the gradients over steps.
Repeated multiplication makes gradients vanish (or explode), so plain RNNs forget long-range context.
Gates fix this: GRU (reset, update) and LSTM (forget, input, output + cell state); bidirectional and stacked variants add context and depth.
thirty: A recurrent neural network processes a sequence one step at a time and carries a hidden state, a running summary of everything seen so far. At each step it combines the previous state with the new input using the same weights every time, so it handles sequences of any length. It's trained by backpropagation through time. Plain RNNs struggle with long-range dependencies because gradients shrink exponentially as they flow back through many steps. GRUs and LSTMs add learned gates that decide what to keep, forget and output; the LSTM's additive cell state lets information and gradients survive hundreds of steps. Variants read in both directions or stack layers, and they're used for language, speech and time-series forecasting.

check.q: What does the hidden state of an RNN represent?
opts: A fixed-size summary of the sequence so far
check.why: h_t = f(x_t, h_{t−1}) compresses the history.

check.q: Why can one RNN process sequences of any length?
opts: It has a weight per position
It shares the same weights across all time steps
